newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila stock market sceptical despite 2-day surge.
newsitem.headline: Manila stock market sceptical despite 2-day surge.

text.p: Manila shares ended on a high note for the second straight day on Thursday, but market players were not convinced that an earlier downtrend had been reversed.
The 30-share main index broke through the 3,000-point resistance level on strong buying in oversold issues.
The index rose by 77.49 points, or 2.60 percent, to 3,061.06 points. On Wednesday, it had risen 56.14 points, or 1.92 percent, to 2,983.57.
Analysts were not convinced the bear spell was over.
"It was too fast. It's a recovery but it has to be tested," said Kevin Khoe, analyst at Sapphire Securities.

"The market has been down for some time and with investors getting used to the drop, they are probably not convinced that it's finally over," said Noel Reyes, research head at Anscor-Hagedorn Securities Inc.
Earlier the Manila index fell by 242.35 points, or 7.64 percent, from the start of the month, closing at a seven-month low of 2,927.43 on Tuesday.
The market's weakness in the face of good local fundamentals gave rise to two theories on the market's fall.

The first was that the heavily capitalised property sector was suffering from the belief that the property boom was over. The other was that foreign funds had pulled out of the Philippines as part of portfolio reshuffling.
But with both the theories now discounted and the weakness still persisting, a cautious attitude is best, analysts said.
On Thursday, the property sector led the rally with the property sub-index rising 4.68 percent, or 6.76 points, to 151.18 points.
Patrick Garcia, vice-president at L.M. Garcia & Associates, said the belief that foreign funds had divested their Philippine portfolios was not correct.
"We have been keeping a watch on the dealing system and there seems to be no indication of big outflows. So all the funds that were supposed to have gone out of the country are still here," he said.
Selective picking of low-priced stocks was the advice offered by most analysts.
Irving Ackerman, president of Irving Ackerman & Co, said: "There seems to be a turnaround but we cannot be certain if it will be sustained."
